evidence: src/controllers/cardsController.ts: create, activate, getStatement, blockCard, unblockCard and createVirtual each read req.body or req.params, call one cardServices method and respond with res.status/res.sendStatus/res.send.

src/controllers/paymentsController.ts: buyOnPointOfSale and buyOnline read req.body, call paymentServices.insertPayment or insertOnlinePayment, then res.sendStatus(200). This is the same handler pattern.
src/controllers/rechargeController.ts: recharge reads cardId and amount from req.body, calls rechargeService.recharge, then res.sendStatus(200).
No validation, business rules or persistence access is repeated or inlined in any controller. Every rule is left to the services.
src/controllers/paymentsController.ts exports the BuyOnPOSBody and BuyOnlineBody body types. The other controllers have no typed bodies. This is a minor style difference, not a split in concerns.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The unit passes. All three files serve the same concern, HTTP request handling. Each one is a set of thin Express handlers that read values from req, call the matching service, and send a status or body back. No business rule or invariant is repeated across the files, and none of them skips the service layer. The handlers never touch repositories or put domain logic inline. There is one small inconsistency: paymentsController.ts declares and exports typed request-body interfaces (BuyOnPOSBody, BuyOnlineBody), while cardsController.ts and rechargeController.ts read req.body without types. The graph also shows paymentServices.ts and onlinePaymentSchema.ts importing those interfaces from the controller. Which way imports point between layers is out of scope for this check. The uneven typing is a style gap, not a split concern, a duplicated invariant or a bypassed abstraction, so it doesn't fail the rubric.
